Other names were Devil's-Hen, Screech-Geer, Bubbling-John, and Blue-Monkey. The Yanks call it Yellow-Hammer, or Yellow-Bird, or Yellow-Poll. This was also called the Devil's Bird, the Devil's Cock, and Satan's Hen.
Yellow-hammers were once known as devil's birds and were believed to have been brought by Satan as a pest.
The Devil's bird is the Yellowhammer, which, with its striking yellow plumage, looks more like a little yellow bird of heaven than an evil spirit.
Yellow-hammer, Devil's bird, as it was also called, was a screaming nuisance when it arrived on Scottish farms in vast numbers.
This species had been known in the past as a ‘peacemaker’, or ‘devil's bird’ or even as the ‘flattened backside’.

The name Devil's bird, which is given in some districts of the north to the yellow-hammered siskin (Emberiza citrinella), has not, to my knowledge, been applied in any other part of the country than west and south-west Scotland.
The devils' bird was another name for the yellowhammer.
Yellowhammers or Devil's Birds were considered evil as they were considered to be portents of evil things to come.

The yellowhammer was known as the Devil's Bird because it did not build its own nests, but pilfered the young of other birds by force.
A yellowhammer was known as the ‘devil's bird’, because it turned the crops to dust with its long beak as it fed at seedtime.
Yellowhammers were called the Devil's Bird as they were said to be harbours of devils and to disturb people.

Yellow-hammers were generally considered to be Devil's Birds or Devil's Sitters, the old names for the birds that brought about ill luck and the worst of weather if one's house was too clean, and ill luck or death if a male or female of the species was killed.

The yellow-hammer was sometimes called the Devil's Bird for its supposed power to frighten away evil spirits from a house, which is a curious usage in view of its strictly nocturnal habits.
